newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Hun Sen shrugs off rising international pressure.
newsitem.headline: Hun Sen shrugs off rising international pressure.

text.p: Cambodia's powerful premier Hun Sen on Friday shrugged off mounting international efforts to solve his country's political crisis and told foreigners, including ASEAN, to stay out of his affairs.
Second Prime Minister Hun Sen said he would meet three envoys from the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) on Saturday, but appeared weary of their diplomatic efforts.
Cambodia, he said, could survive without ASEAN.

"I will sit down and listen to them," he said of the envoys, but added, "No foreigner can control Hun Sen. I will ask them to finish the problem tomorrow so they won't have to bother about Cambodia any more... Please don't interfere."
"If they don't let us join ASEAN, we won't join. If we don't join ASEAN, it won't be the death of us," he said during a visit to a pagoda about 60 km (36 miles) south of Phnom Penh.
Hun Sen said he could take back $1.4 million in membership dues and ASEAN fees and instead build schools in Cambodia.
Hun Sen's comments came as international efforts to solve Cambodia's problems intensified and the United States said it would send an envoy to Asia to help convince Hun Sen to walk a democratic path.

Three ASEAN foreign ministers, including Thailand's Prachuab Chaiyasarn, Indonesia's Ali Alatas and Domingo Siazon of the Philippines, were due to meet ousted First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh in Bangkok on Friday and Hun Sen on Saturday in Phnom Penh.

Hun Sen overthrew Ranariddh nearly two weeks ago in a bloody offensive in the capital that drew criticism from the international community and led to the delay of Cambodia's expected entry into ASEAN later this month.
Since the coup, several nations have put pressure on Hun Sen to end the killings of Ranariddh loyalists and restore the country's coalition government.
Hun Sen seemed irritated that Ranariddh remained an issue for ASEAN.
"You think only about one person and not the general situation. The Paris peace agreement didn't name any one prime minister," he said. "Let us solve our problems by ourselves."
He challenged Ranariddh to return to Cambodia and face accusations of weapons smuggling and illegal ties to the Khmer Rouge guerrillas.
"Now, Norodom Ranariddh is in Bangkok. If (he) is brave enough, please come back and face trial," Hun Sen said.
His speech came as ASEAN was considering possibly admitting Cambodia into the regional club at its 30th anniversary on August 8 or at a summit meeting on December 20, diplomats said.

In an effort to coordinate diplomatic efforts with Asia, the United States announced on Thursday it would send former U.S. congressman Stephen Solarz to Beijing, Tokyo, Bangkok, Jakarta, Kuala Lumpur and Phnom Penh, where he is to meet Hun Sen.

Unlike the United States and ASEAN, Australian Foreign Minister Alexander Downer on Friday steered clear of immediate engagement with Hun Sen. He delayed a planned visit to Cambodia to avoid indicating support for Hun Sen's regime, a spokesman said.
